1.content: Create and run a native QuickGUI app with QuickGUI UI. These guides use Go. Choose TypeScript in the sidebar for Solid 2 JSX. QuickGUI apps are ordinary Go programs. Write components and fine-grained reactive state in Go, then build with CGO_ENABLED=0 . The prebuilt native library is loaded in the same process through purego. Bun runs the CLI for development and packaging.
1.keywords: install create cli window bun macos

2.content: macOS 14 or newer Go 1.23 or newer Bun 1.3 or newer Xcode Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ) The packaged UI application currently targets macOS. Normal application builds use the prebuilt native host.

3.content: The CLI is not published yet. Start from a QuickGUI checkout and run the Go counter: To create a separate app, scaffold without installing registry packages and choose Go when prompted: In the generated quickgui.config.ts , change the defineConfig import to ../quickgui/packages/cli/src/index.ts to use the local CLI. Then run bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts dev --project ../my-app from the QuickGUI checkout. Pass --language go to init to skip the language prompt.

4.content: The generated main.go imports native for windows and ui for components. Pass the component function directly to WindowOptions.Component . Call native.Run once to start the application event loop.

5.content: The watcher rebuilds your Go source and restarts the development app. The formatter gives long component calls consistent line breaks while preserving ordinary Go syntax. Production bundles are written under dist/darwin-* .

6.content: Understand components and signals . Add styles and conditional options . Explore the component reference .

7.content: Understand the files in a generated QuickGUI UI project. A QuickGUI project keeps application code in a Go module and development commands in a small Bun package.

8.content: The CLI generates these files. Commit go.sum after resolving dependencies.

9.content: main.go starts native.Run and creates a window. Components and deferred construction callbacks return *ui.Element or *native.Node . Every created node is returned, assigned, or passed to a parent; implicit declaration blocks are unsupported. Split larger applications into ordinary Go packages.

10.content: entry is the Go package to build. The configuration file is evaluated by the Bun CLI. It is not part of the running application. You can also use quickgui.toml with the same settings: The CLI checks quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . quickgui dev --config configs/dev.toml or quickgui build --config configs/release.toml selects a file explicitly. Relative paths are resolved from the project directory, and dev reloads config edits. Quote version values, for example version = "0.1.0" , and put application fields before the [native] table.

11.content: Use github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/native for windows and platform services, github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui for UI, and github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/reactive for owners and contexts. @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. Pin the Go SDK and CLI to compatible release versions. To share your own components or build an optional native backend, see Authoring Extensions .

12.content: For SDK development, add a local replace directive in go.mod pointing github.com/egoist/quickgui/go to the checkout’s go directory. Run the checkout’s CLI with bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts dev --project path/to/app . Ordinary Go edits reuse the native shared library.

13.content: Add optional Sparkle-compatible updates to a Go application. The optional github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/updater package provides automatic application updates. Importing it includes @quickgui/extension-updater ; apps without the import include neither that library nor Sparkle. Ordinary Go edits reuse the prebuilt native artifacts.
13.keywords: updater sparkle appcast ed25519 extension updates

14.content: Generate an Ed25519 key pair with Bun tooling: Keep the private .key outside version control and copy the contents of .pub into quickgui.toml : The CLI embeds the current version, identifier, target-specific feed URL, default preference, and public key in the Go executable. On macOS it also generates Sparkle's Info.plist settings and signs the nested Sparkle helpers with the app's identity. Secret keys are never embedded. Developer ID apps are supported; App Store and sandboxed builds must exclude the updater import using a Go build tag or platform file.

15.content: Start after native.Run reports readiness, outside components. Share the handle between settings, menus, and any update banner. An updater belongs to the application, so closing a window must not close it. Call updates.Check(done) from a Check for Updates menu item, updates.Install(done) from an available-update banner, and updates.SetAutomaticChecks(enabled, done) from settings. Callbacks always run on the Go UI goroutine. State() reads the latest cached event without calling native code or polling. Initialization and commands report errors through their completion callbacks. Options can override the feed URL and public key. Windows/Linux also allow current version and identifier overrides; Sparkle reads those from the app bundle, and its public key must match the embedded SUPublicEDKey . Development builds are disabled by default, including when using a release-built native library. Use AllowDevelopment: true only with a deliberately configured test feed and disposable app bundle.

16.content: Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, plain-text notes, progress byte counts, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. An explicit check that finds no update reports Kind == "up-to-date" on the portable backend. macOS also uses Sparkle's standard result windows. On macOS, scheduled discoveries are retained for an in-app banner. Manual checks promote a retained result into Sparkle's standard UI. Sparkle owns download, verification, installation, scheduling, and relaunch. Its persisted preference takes precedence over the packaged default. Windows and Linux perform one quiet check per launch when enabled, and another when automatic checking is enabled. There is no idle polling timer. Download progress is throttled to at most ten events per second plus completion. Checks and installation cannot overlap; an explicit check adopts an in-flight automatic check. The portable installer verifies the artifact before preparing a handoff. QuitRequired means the helper has validated its inputs and is waiting for the current process to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after dealing with unsaved work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out after two minutes and leaves the current application intact. Closing an updater cancels checks and pre-handoff downloads; an accepted installer handoff is already owned by the helper.

17.content: Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle 2.9.4, embedded only with the extension Windows QuickGUI NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for app exit, runs the verified installer with /S and the current install directory, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage A helper waits for app exit, replaces the user-owned AppImage atomically, and restores the old image if replacement or startup fails Linux .deb , system binaries, unpacked AppDirs, and root-owned installations report disabled ; use their package manager. A new AppImage must retain the updater import so the SDK can acknowledge startup to the helper. Linux backups are deleted only after that acknowledgement and a short startup grace period. Windows installer failures are reported; rollback remains the installer's responsibility. The portable backend supports HTTPS Sparkle RSS appcasts, raw Ed25519 enclosure signatures, semantic-version ordering, target-specific feeds, and Windows minimum-system requirements. It skips deltas and unsupported channel/rollout constraints. It does not implement every Sparkle feature. Feed reads are limited to 1 MiB, downloads to 512 MiB, and presentation notes to 16 KiB. Signatures and declared lengths are checked again by the installer helper before installation. No unsigned fallback is available.

18.content: Place the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ), using your CI secret store. Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. Keys use Sparkle's current base64-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 seed format and also work with Sparkle's sign_update tool. The CLI signs the finished platform artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed at its configured HTTPS URL. Feeds are per target, so architectures cannot accidentally install each other's binaries. The generated feed contains the current release; it does not generate Sparkle delta archives or staged rollouts. updates.manifest = true enables generation for every production build. macOS archives preserve framework symlinks and should contain the Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows requires makensis ; sign the installer with the configured Authenticode identity. Linux requires appimagetool to produce an updateable AppImage. Public-key mismatches, missing signing keys, missing installers, and unsupported payloads fail the build. Existing Rust users can explicitly enable the legacy updater Cargo feature for the Minisign JSON UpdateClient . It is no longer a default feature or part of the Go native core. That legacy client and its CLI manifest path remain separate from this Sparkle-compatible extension; use updater.Start , not the removed native.Updater facade.

19.content: The builder stages the shared library plus Sparkle resources on macOS, or the installer helper on Windows/Linux. The CLI discovers the import transitively and fetches the exact-version extension package when necessary. End users need only the packaged application. The current npm release matrix ships macOS artifacts. Windows/Linux implementations can be built from source on their target hosts; publishing those prebuilt targets follows the framework's broader platform release support. See the runnable example and native extension contract . Sparkle configuration and appcast details are documented by Sparkle .

20.content: Share Go components and build optional native providers for QuickGUI. An extension can be an ordinary Go package that composes QuickGUI components, or a Go package backed by a separately built native library. Start with Go when the existing UI and platform APIs cover your feature. Add a native extension when you need an optional native dependency, as the terminal and updater packages do.
20.keywords: extension authoring init-extension zig rust plugin native provider third-party purego manifest ABI ServiceApi RequireExtension InvokeExtension OpenExtension npm

21.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Choose an extension type
21.content: What you are adding What you ship Core changes Components, themes, or application logic A Go module None A native service, SDK, or optional backend A Go package, manifest, and native library implementing the service ABI None UI backed by native data A native service plus Go components using existing primitives None Native services register automatically by name. Use your own Go module, npm package or scope, and release cycle. Consumers import your Go package; the CLI discovers its manifest and bundles the selected native artifact. No core registry entry, extension-specific kind, CLI fork, or QuickGUI release-pipeline change is needed. An extension runs in the application's process. The Go application loads the core and selected extensions through purego. Each extension owns its backend dependencies; the core keeps the renderer, layout engine, and native event loop. Go edits reuse these libraries, so consumers do not rebuild the native backend on every edit.

22.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Create an extension project
22.content: go is the default and creates a reusable component with a reactive demo. zig and rust create a standalone native service with a typed Go wrapper, a manifest, vendored ABI definitions, and an npm artifact package. Every template includes cmd/demo and quickgui.toml : Use --module github.com/acme/my-service for your Go module and --npm-package @acme/extension-my-service for a native artifact package. --name overrides the directory-derived extension name. Defaults are example.com/<name> and quickgui-extension-<name> . --no-install skips bun install and go mod tidy ; initialization preserves non-empty directories. The Zig template requires Zig 0.16.x; Rust uses stable Cargo/Rust. Build scripts are TypeScript run with Bun. bun run build builds the native library for the current machine into artifacts/lib/<target>/ . The manifest supplies its identity and release version to the Go wrapper, generated native constants, and npm package. bun run dev builds it once, then reuses it while watching Go edits. Restart after editing native code. Pure Go extensions have no native build step or artifact package. Before the packages are published, use bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts init-extension <directory> --type <type> --no-install from this checkout. Set the generated Go SDK requirement to the local go directory with a replace directive and the CLI dependency to a local file: path, then install dependencies. The generated README describes development and publishing.

23.content: Create a module under your own repository path, depend on the Go SDK, and export component functions. This package needs neither a native manifest nor an npm package: Return notice.Notice(message, ui.Style().Padding(16)) or pass its result as a child. The accessor stays reactive, and the caller's style merges after the defaults. Component functions and deferred construction callbacks must return a node. Use ui.OnCleanup for resources owned by a mounted component; keep application-wide services outside component ownership. Publish the module using Go version tags, and document the SDK versions you support. Consumers add it with go get using your module path. Transitive imports of terminal or updater still opt the application into those native extensions, so keep optional integrations in separate packages or build-tagged files.

24.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
24.content: The working native-extension example pairs a Go package with a small C library named acme-echo . It builds against the standalone C ABI header , with no renderer or core crate dependency. In your own repository, use a layout such as: Vendor the small header into your project. C, C++, Rust, and other languages that export a C ABI can implement an extension. Rust extensions can vendor the equivalent extension_api.rs layouts and build a cdylib , without linking quickgui , quickgui-host , WGPU, or Taffy. The updater backend demonstrates an asynchronous service. The extension in this guide uses its own release 1.0.0 . Its descriptor, manifest, npm package, and RequireExtension version must agree. The service ABI version and table layout determine core compatibility; the extension's release does not need to match QuickGUI's release. Document the Go SDK and service ABI versions your package requires. The built-in terminal's typed rendering contract remains tied to its matching core release.

25.content: Place this manifest beside the imported Go package's source , not just at the module root or in application configuration: Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. Choose a distinctive name; host is reserved and terminal uses its built-in typed contract. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores, without lib or a file extension. The npm package may use any valid scope or be unscoped. The manifest is limited to 16 KiB, and an application can require at most 32 extensions. The Go package declares the matching release during initialization and exposes a typed operation: RequireExtension only records a requirement. Do not load libraries, open windows, or start workers in init . Call operations after native.Run reports readiness, on the UI goroutine. Replies also run there. native.InvokeExtension sends any JSON-encodable value and returns the extension's JSON result, preserving explicit null members. Methods start with an ASCII letter and contain up to 64 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores, or hyphens. For a persistent service, call native.OpenExtension(name, options, changed, ready) and wait for its successful ready callback. Use session.Request("lookup", value, done) for a JSON result, or session.Command when only an error is needed. Each command has its own reply; events remain subscribed until session.Close() . Close on the UI goroutine when the owner is disposed. Reserve start and stop for session lifecycle. Wrap these low-level calls with typed options, events, and methods in your public package. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps , using the same entry package, target, and build tags as compilation. Transitive imports count; excluded files do not. Both the manifest and the RequireExtension call are needed: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

26.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
26.content: Export quickgui_extension_v1 with C linkage and default symbol visibility. It returns a static descriptor containing your name, exact extension version, ABI version 1 , service kind 2 , and a two-function table. All services share this kind; do not invent a new kind per extension. The public header defines every field and callback signature. A Rust service implements ServiceApi.invoke and ServiceApi.shutdown . This descriptor fragment uses a local copy of the ABI definitions: Only C layouts, fixed-width fields, borrowed byte spans, and function pointers cross the boundary. Keep language-owned objects and allocator ownership inside their library. The descriptor, strings, and table have static lifetimes. Copy borrowed request bytes before retaining them, enqueue slow work, and return immediately. Do not wait for network I/O, worker completion, or native main-thread execution. Bound queues, active sessions, and retained data; catch recoverable panics before crossing an extern "C" boundary. The Go session protocol is: Request Parameters Extension responsibility A one-shot method such as echo The value passed to InvokeExtension Reply once, then release its sink start The options JSON passed to OpenExtension Use the request ID as the session ID; reply and retain its event sink A command such as send {"session": 123, "value": "hello"} Find that session and settle this command's own reply stop {"session": 123} Stop accepting work for that session, cancel its resources, and reply shutdown function No parameters Cancel all sessions without blocking the UI thread ServiceSink.emit kind 0 carries one successful JSON reply, kind 1 a UTF-8 error, and kind 2 a JSON session event. Use null for success without a result. Request and emitted payloads are each limited to 64 KiB. Payload bytes are borrowed only during emit ; the host copies them into its existing event queue. Workers may emit from any thread. Schedule OS APIs that require the main thread on that thread without blocking the calling Go goroutine. The start sink stays alive after the start reply so it can deliver events. Command sinks are separate. Call each sink's release exactly once, including errors and rejected work, after its final callback. Closing a session must suppress later events and release workers; keeping a library loaded must not keep its sessions alive. Extension images remain loaded for process lifetime because callbacks may still reference their function pointers. The C echo implementation shows the complete one-shot contract. For visual features, publish changed data to reactive Go components built from existing QuickGUI primitives. The service ABI does not add custom renderer node kinds; a new rendering primitive still requires a renderer implementation.

27.content: Before application startup, the Go loader opens each selected image, calls its exported entry point, and passes the descriptor and required version to the core. The core validates the header before reading its layout, then checks the name, release, ABI, table size, and non-null callbacks. It stores service tables by name and automatically routes extension/acme-echo/<method> requests and application shutdown. Identical registrations are idempotent. Different versions or tables under the same name are rejected, and the CLI also rejects conflicting npm packages under that name. Extension callbacks run outside the registry lock. The registry and loaded images persist for the process lifetime; your shutdown function must cancel all remaining sessions. There is no extension-specific registry code to edit.

28.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
28.content: Use TypeScript scripts run with Bun to build native artifacts once. The example's build-extension.ts compiles its C extension directly with Clang and stages the current host target. A Rust extension can invoke Cargo from its own repository in the same way: Set the Rust library name to quickgui_acme_echo and its crate type to cdylib . Run bun build-extension.ts on each supported host. This script does not cross-compile. Target directories are darwin-arm64 , darwin-x64 , linux-arm64 , linux-x64 , windows-arm64 , and windows-x64 . Ship only targets you build and validate. The native npm package contains artifacts and exposes its metadata for the resolver: Replace @acme with your own scope. Publish this artifact package with your own release workflow and keep it optional; the Go import selects it. Your build script and releases are independent of QuickGUI's built-in --extension command and version synchronization. Consumers reuse your prebuilts during Go edits. If your extension needs helper executables or resources, declare their basenames in a manifest resources object keyed by darwin , linux , or windows . Each platform accepts up to 16 distinct files; the same platform list applies to both architectures. Put those files next to the library in every applicable target directory. The CLI copies them alongside the native libraries and marks plain resource executables as executable. Directory resources use .qgr bundles produced by the repository's packResources helper. It preserves executable modes and confined relative symlinks with entry and byte limits. Resource paths cannot overwrite core or extension images. macOS frameworks must also satisfy the platform's signing requirements. Sparkle resources receive the existing macOS signing and bundle configuration; other services do not need updater settings.

29.content: Try the standalone example from a QuickGUI checkout: For your own consumer, add your Go module with go get , import its package, and run quickgui dev or quickgui build . Install the matching native npm package for offline or private distribution, or let the CLI fetch the exact release from the public npm registry. For development, set QUICKGUI_EXTENSION_DIR to the absolute target artifact directory. This override must contain every required library and resource, including transitive requirements. Resolution checks the explicit directory, installed npm package, then exact-version npm download; source-checkout fallback applies only to QuickGUI's built-in packages. Downloads require SHA-512 integrity, only declared artifacts are extracted, and caches include the npm package identity. Private registry downloads are not automatic; install private packages with your package manager first. Before shipping, verify these behaviors: An app without the import bundles no extension or optional backend dependencies. Adding and removing a transitive import changes a fresh bundle correctly. The bundled executable loads the extension through purego with the matching core. Missing files, names, ABI versions, release versions, and conflicting requirements produce errors. Starting, closing before startup finishes, repeated closing, cancellation, and application shutdown release every callback context and worker. Events stop after disposal. Background work never blocks the UI. Clean sessions sleep; queues, snapshots, caches, and resource payloads have limits. Follow the performance guide . bun pm pack includes every library and resource your manifest declares. Install the resulting archive into a separate consumer, build with native source staging unavailable, and exercise it on each supported OS and architecture. The repository's scripts/check-extensions.ts builds the independent C extension, exercises its real replies through purego, and bundles a separate consumer with its own Go module and npm scope. It also checks the built-in extensions and their combinations. Add equivalent checks to your extension repository. End users receive the packaged application with all selected libraries; they need no Bun, Cargo, npm packages, or native toolchain to run it.

30.content: Manage window lifetimes and asynchronous native work. Call native.Run once from main . Its startup callback creates windows and registers application services. Native completion callbacks and UI state changes run on the Go UI goroutine.
30.keywords: window native lifecycle services WatchFiles Dispatch Async

31.content: native.NewWindow(native.WindowOptions{Component: App}) creates a window with its own component owner and retained tree. Closing the window disposes its bindings, listeners, and component cleanup. Capture native.CurrentWindow() while constructing a component or handling an event when later work needs its window handle.

32.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Commands and services
32.content: Use the typed native APIs for dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, and other platform services. Operations with results use completion callbacks; handle their errors without blocking the UI goroutine. Independent extensions use native.InvokeExtension and native.OpenExtension . For application background work, use ui.Async with component cancellation or native.Dispatch to return results to the UI goroutine. Read and write signals only there. See Authoring Extensions for service and session ownership.

33.hierarchy: Windows & Native Services › Events and file watching
33.content: native.WatchFiles(paths, changed, ready) uses operating-system file notifications and returns a stop function. Register component resources with ui.OnCleanup , and retain cancellation functions for application-scoped listeners. Avoid polling when a native event or watcher is available. Extension session events stop when their session closes.

34.content: Signals connect state to the text and properties that read it. Updates change retained nodes without rerunning the entire component.
34.keywords: signal reactivity memo effect batch cleanup

35.content: Read signals directly in component text and fluent properties, such as ui.Text("Count: ", count()) and .Width(width()) . Custom components accept ordinary int , string , and struct parameters; calling LineItem(product, quantity()) preserves its live inputs. The QuickGUI CLI generates the internal getters and bindings automatically. Setup assignments such as initial := count() remain snapshots. Explicit accessors are still supported, and are required when using raw Go commands that bypass the view compiler. Event handlers batch writes automatically. Use ui.Batch for a group of writes elsewhere, and ui.CreateMemo for derived values. String and numeric signals can be children directly: ui.Text("Count: ", count) . The prefix stays retained while only the number updates. Numeric bindings use strconv ; they do not parse a format string. For a combined string property, use strconv.Itoa(count()) and concatenation inside an accessor.

36.content: Use ui.CreateMemo for a value computed from other signals. It returns an accessor, so consumers subscribe to the derived value just like any other signal.

37.content: Use ui.CreateEffect to synchronize a side effect with the signals it reads. Dependencies follow the reads made during each run, including conditional branches. Register teardown with ui.OnCleanup ; disposing the owning component releases its effects and subscriptions. Bind changing text and props directly instead of rebuilding a view inside an effect. Use an effect for work outside the view tree, such as synchronizing a subscription or updating a native window title. The effect runs initially and again when a value it read changes. Cleanup registered inside that effect runs before the next execution and when its owner is disposed. This example logs the lifecycle; replace the log calls with your subscription’s start and stop operations. Capture the topic for that execution so cleanup refers to the old topic.

38.content: Event handlers batch signal writes automatically. Wrap related writes elsewhere in ui.Batch(func() { ... }) so dependent work flushes together. ui.Untrack reads state without subscribing the current computation. Signal access belongs on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async or native.Dispatch to deliver background results. Here both fields change as one update. Observers see “Grace Hopper” after the batch rather than an intermediate “Grace Lovelace”. The button handler already batches automatically; the explicit batch also makes applyProfile safe to call from other UI code. Batches are synchronous: background work must dispatch its results back before writing signals. The logging examples use Go’s standard log package.

39.content: Components construct a retained tree once when mounted. Reactive bindings update the affected nodes; the native core handles layout, painting, and accessibility.
39.keywords: rendering retained children mount lifecycle keyed

40.content: Every component and UI construction callback returns *ui.Element or *native.Node . Pass nodes directly as children, or return a ui.Fragment(...) for multiple siblings. The compiler rejects discarded UI construction calls and void declaration blocks. Event and effect callbacks retain their normal signatures. Use ui.Show and ui.For for reactive child structure.

41.content: Use ui.Show when state should mount or remove children. A normal Go if runs only during construction. Branch children keep their nodes while the condition stays in the same branch, and disposal removes their bindings.

42.content: Use ui.For for a reactive list and provide stable, unique keys. Use ui.KeyedFor when retained rows need an accessor to changing item data. Removed rows release their subscriptions; moving a keyed row preserves its native identity. Virtualized tables and lists keep large collections bounded to visible rows. Use a database ID or another stable identity as the key, not an item’s position. In this example reordering moves the existing rows, and renaming item 1 updates its label through the row accessor. The parent does not recreate the list. Pass a new slice when editing data so the signal receives the update; mutating a previously stored slice in place does not notify subscribers.

43.content: WindowOptions.Component creates one reactive root per window. Closing the window disposes its nodes and effects. Register resource cleanup with ui.OnCleanup . For background work, ui.Async delivers its result back to the UI goroutine and cancels when its component is disposed. Start background work while its component is mounting. The load function runs away from the UI goroutine and must respect its context; the completion callback can safely write signals. Removing this component’s owning branch or closing its window cancels the context and suppresses late completion. This example uses the standard context package.

44.content: Capture native.CurrentWindow() while the component is mounting, then use the captured window in callbacks. Do not look it up from an unrelated goroutine. Window events and native requests expose asynchronous callbacks.

45.content: Run quickgui test from the app module to test the same compiled views used by development builds. Use quickgui fmt --check to check source formatting. The application is a native Go executable, so ordinary Go diagnostics and debugging tools use the original source files.

46.content: Choose between primitives and accessible compound components. QuickGUI combines unstyled primitives with accessible compound controls. Compose both through ordinary Go functions.
46.keywords: view text button tabs checkbox unstyled

47.content: A Go component returns *ui.Element or *native.Node . Use plain typed props and compose children directly. The return type identifies the component, so CounterLabel(count()) stays reactive without annotations or a ui.View(func() { ... }) wrapper. Window roots accept the component function directly. Struct props use ordinary Go types too. Updating quantity changes the bound text while LineItem and its nodes remain mounted. Containers can accept children directly, as shown below. A children callback is optional and runs once when mounted; use it when construction must happen lazily or inside a compound control’s context. Event handlers remain callbacks.

48.content: Start with ui.View , ui.Text , ui.Button , and ui.Input . Pass content or children to constructors, then chain styles, properties, and handlers. Return a node from component functions and deferred child callbacks.

49.content: Compound families expose parts such as ui.Tabs.Root , ui.Tabs.List , and ui.Tabs.Panel . The core handles roles, keyboard navigation, focus, and control state. Create a part inside its root’s children callback so its context exists.

50.content: A controlled value is an accessor; its callback stores the value accepted by the control. Use a default value to let the component own its state. Optional scalar values use pointers, while multiple selections use slices.

51.content: The reference covers forms, pickers, layout and data, overlays, menus, and routing. examples/components contains all 42 original gallery demos, including a 5,000-row table and lazy tree. The separate examples/swift-ui gallery demonstrates native SwiftUI hosting.

52.content: Use PartProps.Style for each part. Build styles with ui.Style() and fluent modifiers; combine shared builders with .Merge(...) . Parts also accept slices of builders and accessors returning them. Selection and theme signals update retained parts without rebuilding children. Every native control has a dedicated page in the Components sidebar. For complete workflows, see Forms & Input and Overlays & Dialogs .

53.content: The router selects components from the current application path and keeps a navigation history. Routes render native QuickGUI content in the current window.
53.keywords: router route layout outlet navigation history parameters

54.content: Declare routes with ui.Route and ui.Layout . A layout mounts its matched child with ui.Outlet . Read parameters with ui.UseParams , or navigate with ui.UseRouter .

55.content: Wrap related routes in ui.Layout . Its component calls ui.Outlet() where the matched child belongs. Navigation between sibling routes keeps their common layout mounted, preserving its state. Only the changed route branch is replaced. Keep shared navigation outside the outlet. Its local state survives switching between Home and Settings because both routes share the same layout. The outlet supplies only the active child.

56.content: Inside a route component, ui.UseRouter() exposes Navigate , Replace , Back , and Forward . ui.Link declares a navigation target. Pushes add a history entry; replacing changes the current entry.

57.content: Read matched path parameters with ui.UseParams , query values with ui.UseSearchParams , and the current location with ui.UseLocation . These return accessors; read them inside a binding when the displayed value should update. A parameter-only change keeps the matched route component mounted. A :name segment captures one path parameter. Keep reads inside text accessors: capturing params()["name"] during setup would leave the label at its initial value. Query parameters are separate from path parameters. This route initially displays quickgui and history .

58.content: Lay out and style native nodes with familiar properties. Go elements and ui.Style() share fluent style modifiers, including .P4() , .MxAuto() , .GridCols(3) , and .RoundedLg() . Pass children to constructors and apply reusable styles with .Style(shared) .
58.keywords: style layout flexbox grid color hover

59.content: Declarations apply in order. Later values override the same property, including explicit zero. Numeric lengths are logical pixels; strings also accept percentages.

60.content: .Style(base).Style(overrides) merges declarations in order. Use .Merge(...) to compose reusable builders. Repeated interaction states merge their properties too.

61.content: ui.Style() returns a ui.StyleBuilder . Modifiers return new values, leaving shared styles unchanged. Assign the result when deriving a style. Apply it with .Style(...) or a compound part’s PartProps.Style field; parts also accept slices of builders and accessors returning them. Scalar accessors stay reactive and bind independently on each mounted node. .When(condition, func(s ui.StyleBuilder) ui.StyleBuilder { ... }) conditionally derives a builder from a boolean value. For a reactive condition, use the element’s .When(getter, style) or evaluate the builder inside a part’s style accessor. Pass scalar signal getters to modifiers, such as .Width(width) ; calling width() during setup captures its current value.

62.content: Use .Flex() , .FlexRow() , or .FlexCol() to select a flex layout. Give scrolling flex children .MinHeight(0) or .MinWidth(0) so they can shrink.

63.content: Grid accepts track strings and the same Rust layout helpers on elements and style builders.

64.content: Typography inherits through the node tree. Colors accept hex, rgb() / rgba() , or packed RGBA values. Override only the child properties that differ. Padding and borders do not inherit.

65.content: Elements and style builders use callbacks for .Hover(...) , .Active(...) , .FocusStyle(...) , .DisabledStyle(...) , and .SelectedStyle(...) . These states run in the native core. Add .Transition(...) to the base style to animate paint changes; see Transitions & Animation .

66.hierarchy: Styling & Layout › Groups and named group hover
66.content: .Group(true) marks an unnamed group; .Group("card") names it. .GroupHover(...) follows the nearest ancestor group, while .GroupHoverNamed("card", ...) follows the nearest ancestor with that name. Repeated rules accumulate in declaration order; a node’s own hover style wins for overlapping properties. .GroupActive(...) and .GroupActiveNamed(...) follow pressed groups. .FocusWithin(...) follows focus in the node or a descendant. These states accept paint properties and cannot set the cursor. Hovering group padding or descendants activates the rules without rerunning components.

67.content: Animate native style changes and images with retained Go components. Animate changes to retained nodes with ui.Style().Transition(...) . The native runtime advances the frames; your component does not rerun for every frame. Import ui from github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui .
67.keywords: transition animation easing duration hover opacity reduced motion gif webp

68.content: Put the transition on the base style so it applies when the pointer enters and leaves. The same declaration works with other paint states, including Active , Focus , Expanded , and DragOver .

69.content: Use a signal or ui.When to change the target. The card below keeps the same node and children while its color and opacity animate. Updating the target during a transition starts from its current visible value, including when reversing direction.

70.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
70.content: Use ui.TransitionDeclaration when several properties share one timing configuration. Import time for the duration in this example. Pass longhand transition props directly to the primitive: Field Usage ui.Style().TransitionProperty(...) A comma-separated string or []string of supported property names. ui.Style().TransitionDuration(...) Milliseconds as a number, a time.Duration , or a string such as "180ms" or "0.18s" . The host bounds durations to 0–10 seconds. ui.Style().TransitionEasing(...) "linear" , "ease" , "ease-in" , "ease-out" , or "ease-in-out" . "ease" aliases the default "ease-in-out" ; these select QuickGUI curves. ui.Style().TransitionTimingFunction(...) Alias for ui.Style().TransitionEasing(...) . ui.Style().TransitionMaxFps(...) Optional frame-rate cap. Omit it to follow display presentation; completion still occurs at the transition deadline. A node has one duration, easing, and frame-rate cap for all selected properties. Comma-separated shorthand entries collect property names; the last duration and easing apply to the entire list. Delays, cubic-bezier() , and independent timings per property are not supported. Explicit longhand fields override the shorthand. A duration alone, such as ui.Style().Transition(180 * time.Millisecond) , transitions background, border, and text colors. Select "all" explicitly to include all supported paint properties. Use ui.Style().Transition("none") to remove the shorthand declaration.

71.content: Transition name Go style prop background-color or background ui.Style().BackgroundColor(...) or a solid ui.Style().Background(...) border-color ui.Style().BorderColor(...) border-width ui.Style().BorderWidth(...) and edge widths border-radius ui.Style().BorderRadius(...) and corner radii color Inherited ui.Style().TextColor(...) opacity Subtree ui.Style().Opacity(...) box-shadow ui.Style().BoxShadow(...) transform Subtree ui.Style().Transform(...) , including translation, scale, and rotation "all" means these properties. Gradient stops, width, height, padding, and other layout values do not interpolate through Transition . Unsupported transition property names are rejected. For a sliding switch thumb, use ui.Style().Transform("translateX(20px)") and ui.Style().Transition("transform 160ms ease-out") , then change the target to "translateX(0px)" when unchecked. This moves the painted subtree and its hit area without moving neighboring layout. Transforms interpolate their affine translation, scale, shear, and shortest rotation; TransformOrigin itself changes immediately. The Go UI API exposes paint transitions and animated images. CSS keyframes, timeline callbacks, and spring declarations are not Go style props.

72.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
72.content: A transition animates a change on an existing node; initial styles are applied directly. Keep the node mounted while changing its target. ui.Show removes its children when false and does not wait for an exit fade. Opacity zero alone keeps layout and input behavior. For dialogs, ui.DialogRootProps.EnterDuration and ExitDuration control transition completion and closing-content lifetime; OnOpenChangeComplete reports completion. Those durations do not create visual styles by themselves. See Dialog . Transitions respect the system's Reduce Motion preference. native.WindowOptions.ReduceMotion accepts a *bool for an explicit window policy; leave it nil to follow the system. Motion resolves to its target under Reduce Motion. Hidden or occluded windows pause local transitions, and completed transitions stop requesting frames.

73.content: Pass an animated GIF or WebP path to ui.Image . The native decoder retains the frames and the file's repeat policy; no Go timer or per-frame signal is needed. The path must resolve to an available file, or you can pass a data URL. Package file assets with the CLI's resources option. See Image and project configuration .

74.content: Build controlled fields, choices, and selection controls. Keep field values in signals and write accepted changes back from callbacks.
74.keywords: input field checkbox radio select events

75.content: ui.Input and ui.TextArea host native text editors. Bind ui.Value to an accessor and update it from event.Value in OnInput . OnSubmit handles Return in a single-line input.

76.content: Field.Root associates a label, control, description, and error. Set Required , Invalid , and ValidationMessage from application state. ValidationMode and ValidationDebounceTime configure when the core requests validation; your application owns the validation rule.

77.content: Checkboxes accept bool or ui.CheckedIndeterminate through ui.CheckedState . Radio groups keep one value; checkbox and toggle groups can keep several. Read-only controls remain distinct from disabled controls.

78.content: Declare picker options through PickerSourceProps.Items . Select uses a chosen value; Combobox combines text filtering and selection; Autocomplete accepts free-form input. Multiple pickers use Values and OnValuesChange .

79.content: Plain buttons accept ui.OnClick(func() { ... }) . Use ui.OnClickEvent when you need *native.Event . Compound callbacks use typed values and include the native event when relevant. Keep UI state updates on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async for background work.

80.content: Present in-window overlays and operating-system dialogs. Use a QuickGUI overlay for application-styled content, or a native dialog for platform file picking and alerts.
80.keywords: popover dialog overlay alert file picker

81.content: A popover composes a trigger, positioner, and popup. The side is a preference; the core resolves collisions. Read the result through ui.UsePopoverPlacement inside the root.

82.content: Create modal content under Dialog.Portal . Dialog.Title and Dialog.Description provide its accessible name and description. AlertDialog adds confirmation semantics. Controlled roots receive both the next open state and its reason.

83.content: ui.SystemPopover hosts its body in an operating-system popover. Specify its logical width and height, then declare ordinary QuickGUI children.

84.content: Native dialogs use asynchronous callbacks. Capture the parent window while rendering and pass it explicitly to the request. A canceled open panel returns Canceled: true .

85.content: Mount real SwiftUI controls inside a QuickGUI UI application. The ui.SwiftUI family embeds real macOS controls in a Go application. Ordinary QuickGUI components work without it.
85.keywords: swiftui host slider toggle picker native

86.content: Create controls inside ui.SwiftUI.Host . The host defines the native view boundary and can size itself from its content.

87.content: Available controls include Button, Slider, Toggle, ProgressView, Stepper, TextField, SecureField, Picker, SegmentedControl, DatePicker, ColorPicker, and Gauge. Their platform appearance comes from macOS.

88.content: Bind an accessor and store the value returned by the native callback. A SwiftUI control and a QuickGUI node can share the same signal. DatePicker uses Unix timestamps in milliseconds.

89.content: MatchContents: true sizes both axes intrinsically. Use ui.SwiftUIMatchContents{Vertical: true} for an intrinsic height with an application-defined width in PartProps.Style .

90.content: SwiftUI hosting requires macOS. The prebuilt native host includes the bridge; your Go application still builds without CGO. Native styles can vary with the operating-system version.

91.content: Style SwiftUI controls and host QuickGUI content back inside them. SwiftUI modifiers style native controls. Reverse hosting puts an ordinary QuickGUI subtree inside SwiftUI.
91.keywords: modifier glass quickguihostview popover reverse host

92.content: Apply modifier factories from ui.SwiftUI in order through Modifiers . Available factories include ButtonStyle, ButtonBorderShape, ControlSize, LabelStyle, Tint, and Disabled.

93.content: On supported systems, request the native glass button style with ui.SwiftUI.ButtonStyle("glass") . macOS owns the final appearance.

94.content: ui.SwiftUI.QuickGUIHostView owns a QuickGUI subtree inside the native hierarchy. Provide its size and declare children in a callback so they mount under the embedded window’s lifecycle.

95.content: The SwiftUI popover composes a native trigger through Render . Its content can reverse-host interactive QuickGUI components.

96.content: The host creates its embedded surface after the owner window is mounted and closes it when removed. Declare reverse-hosted children inside the provided callback so their bindings and resources belong to that embedded window. Do not move retained nodes between windows.

.Group(true) marks an unnamed group; .Group("card") names it. .GroupHover(...) follows the nearest ancestor group, while .GroupHoverNamed("card", ...) follows the nearest ancestor with that name. Repeated rules accumulate in declaration order; a node’s own hover style wins for overlapping properties. .GroupActive(...) and .GroupActiveNamed(...) follow pressed groups. .FocusWithin(...) follows focus in the node or a descendant. These states accept paint properties and cannot set the cursor. Hovering group padding or descendants activates the rules without rerunning components.
.Style(base).Style(overrides) merges declarations in order. Use .Merge(...) to compose reusable builders. Repeated interaction states merge their properties too.

A controlled value is an accessor; its callback stores the value accepted by the control. Use a default value to let the component own its state. Optional scalar values use pointers, while multiple selections use slices.

A Go component returns *ui.Element or *native.Node . Use plain typed props and compose children directly. The return type identifies the component, so CounterLabel(count()) stays reactive without annotations or a ui.View(func() { ... }) wrapper. Window roots accept the component function directly. Struct props use ordinary Go types too. Updating quantity changes the bound text while LineItem and its nodes remain mounted. Containers can accept children directly, as shown below. A children callback is optional and runs once when mounted; use it when construction must happen lazily or inside a compound control’s context. Event handlers remain callbacks.

A transition animates a change on an existing node; initial styles are applied directly. Keep the node mounted while changing its target. ui.Show removes its children when false and does not wait for an exit fade. Opacity zero alone keeps layout and input behavior. For dialogs, ui.DialogRootProps.EnterDuration and ExitDuration control transition completion and closing-content lifetime; OnOpenChangeComplete reports completion. Those durations do not create visual styles by themselves. See Dialog . Transitions respect the system's Reduce Motion preference. native.WindowOptions.ReduceMotion accepts a *bool for an explicit window policy; leave it nil to follow the system. Motion resolves to its target under Reduce Motion. Hidden or occluded windows pause local transitions, and completed transitions stop requesting frames.
A virtualized hierarchical collection with expansion, selection, and keyboard navigation.
A virtualized tabular collection with header, row, and cell parts.

Before application startup, the Go loader opens each selected image, calls its exported entry point, and passes the descriptor and required version to the core. The core validates the header before reading its layout, then checks the name, release, ABI, table size, and non-null callbacks. It stores service tables by name and automatically routes extension/acme-echo/<method> requests and application shutdown. Identical registrations are idempotent. Different versions or tables under the same name are rejected, and the CLI also rejects conflicting npm packages under that name. Extension callbacks run outside the registry lock. The registry and loaded images persist for the process lifetime; your shutdown function must cancel all remaining sessions. There is no extension-specific registry code to edit.
Bind an accessor and store the value returned by the native callback. A SwiftUI control and a QuickGUI node can share the same signal. DatePicker uses Unix timestamps in milliseconds.
Build controlled fields, choices, and selection controls. Keep field values in signals and write accepted changes back from callbacks.

Create a module under your own repository path, depend on the Go SDK, and export component functions. This package needs neither a native manifest nor an npm package: Return notice.Notice(message, ui.Style().Padding(16)) or pass its result as a child. The accessor stays reactive, and the caller's style merges after the defaults. Component functions and deferred construction callbacks must return a node. Use ui.OnCleanup for resources owned by a mounted component; keep application-wide services outside component ownership. Publish the module using Go version tags, and document the SDK versions you support. Consumers add it with go get using your module path. Transitive imports of terminal or updater still opt the application into those native extensions, so keep optional integrations in separate packages or build-tagged files.

Create and run a native QuickGUI app with QuickGUI UI. These guides use Go. Choose TypeScript in the sidebar for Solid 2 JSX. QuickGUI apps are ordinary Go programs. Write components and fine-grained reactive state in Go, then build with CGO_ENABLED=0 . The prebuilt native library is loaded in the same process through purego. Bun runs the CLI for development and packaging.
Create controls inside ui.SwiftUI.Host . The host defines the native view boundary and can size itself from its content.

Create modal content under Dialog.Portal . Dialog.Title and Dialog.Description provide its accessible name and description. AlertDialog adds confirmation semantics. Controlled roots receive both the next open state and its reason.

entry is the Go package to build. The configuration file is evaluated by the Bun CLI. It is not part of the running application. You can also use quickgui.toml with the same settings: The CLI checks quickgui.toml before quickgui.config.ts . quickgui dev --config configs/dev.toml or quickgui build --config configs/release.toml selects a file explicitly. Relative paths are resolved from the project directory, and dev reloads config edits. Quote version values, for example version = "0.1.0" , and put application fields before the [native] table.

Event handlers batch signal writes automatically. Wrap related writes elsewhere in ui.Batch(func() { ... }) so dependent work flushes together. ui.Untrack reads state without subscribing the current computation. Signal access belongs on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async or native.Dispatch to deliver background results. Here both fields change as one update. Observers see “Grace Hopper” after the batch rather than an intermediate “Grace Lovelace”. The button handler already batches automatically; the explicit batch also makes applyProfile safe to call from other UI code. Batches are synchronous: background work must dispatch its results back before writing signals. The logging examples use Go’s standard log package.

Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, plain-text notes, progress byte counts, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. An explicit check that finds no update reports Kind == "up-to-date" on the portable backend. macOS also uses Sparkle's standard result windows. On macOS, scheduled discoveries are retained for an in-app banner. Manual checks promote a retained result into Sparkle's standard UI. Sparkle owns download, verification, installation, scheduling, and relaunch. Its persisted preference takes precedence over the packaged default. Windows and Linux perform one quiet check per launch when enabled, and another when automatic checking is enabled. There is no idle polling timer. Download progress is throttled to at most ten events per second plus completion. Checks and installation cannot overlap; an explicit check adopts an in-flight automatic check. The portable installer verifies the artifact before preparing a handoff. QuitRequired means the helper has validated its inputs and is waiting for the current process to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after dealing with unsaved work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out after two minutes and leaves the current application intact. Closing an updater cancels checks and pre-handoff downloads; an accepted installer handoff is already owned by the helper.

Every component and UI construction callback returns *ui.Element or *native.Node . Pass nodes directly as children, or return a ui.Fragment(...) for multiple siblings. The compiler rejects discarded UI construction calls and void declaration blocks. Event and effect callbacks retain their normal signatures. Use ui.Show and ui.For for reactive child structure.

Export quickgui_extension_v1 with C linkage and default symbol visibility. It returns a static descriptor containing your name, exact extension version, ABI version 1 , service kind 2 , and a two-function table. All services share this kind; do not invent a new kind per extension. The public header defines every field and callback signature. A Rust service implements ServiceApi.invoke and ServiceApi.shutdown . This descriptor fragment uses a local copy of the ABI definitions: Only C layouts, fixed-width fields, borrowed byte spans, and function pointers cross the boundary. Keep language-owned objects and allocator ownership inside their library. The descriptor, strings, and table have static lifetimes. Copy borrowed request bytes before retaining them, enqueue slow work, and return immediately. Do not wait for network I/O, worker completion, or native main-thread execution. Bound queues, active sessions, and retained data; catch recoverable panics before crossing an extern "C" boundary. The Go session protocol is: Request Parameters Extension responsibility A one-shot method such as echo The value passed to InvokeExtension Reply once, then release its sink start The options JSON passed to OpenExtension Use the request ID as the session ID; reply and retain its event sink A command such as send {"session": 123, "value": "hello"} Find that session and settle this command's own reply stop {"session": 123} Stop accepting work for that session, cancel its resources, and reply shutdown function No parameters Cancel all sessions without blocking the UI thread ServiceSink.emit kind 0 carries one successful JSON reply, kind 1 a UTF-8 error, and kind 2 a JSON session event. Use null for success without a result. Request and emitted payloads are each limited to 64 KiB. Payload bytes are borrowed only during emit ; the host copies them into its existing event queue. Workers may emit from any thread. Schedule OS APIs that require the main thread on that thread without blocking the calling Go goroutine. The start sink stays alive after the start reply so it can deliver events. Command sinks are separate. Call each sink's release exactly once, including errors and rejected work, after its final callback. Closing a session must suppress later events and release workers; keeping a library loaded must not keep its sessions alive. Extension images remain loaded for process lifetime because callbacks may still reference their function pointers. The C echo implementation shows the complete one-shot contract. For visual features, publish changed data to reactive Go components built from existing QuickGUI primitives. The service ABI does not add custom renderer node kinds; a new rendering primitive still requires a renderer implementation.

For SDK development, add a local replace directive in go.mod pointing github.com/egoist/quickgui/go to the checkout’s go directory. Run the checkout’s CLI with bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts dev --project path/to/app . Ordinary Go edits reuse the native shared library.

Generate an Ed25519 key pair with Bun tooling: Keep the private .key outside version control and copy the contents of .pub into quickgui.toml : The CLI embeds the current version, identifier, target-specific feed URL, default preference, and public key in the Go executable. On macOS it also generates Sparkle's Info.plist settings and signs the nested Sparkle helpers with the app's identity. Secret keys are never embedded. Developer ID apps are supported; App Store and sandboxed builds must exclude the updater import using a Go build tag or platform file.

go is the default and creates a reusable component with a reactive demo. zig and rust create a standalone native service with a typed Go wrapper, a manifest, vendored ABI definitions, and an npm artifact package. Every template includes cmd/demo and quickgui.toml : Use --module github.com/acme/my-service for your Go module and --npm-package @acme/extension-my-service for a native artifact package. --name overrides the directory-derived extension name. Defaults are example.com/<name> and quickgui-extension-<name> . --no-install skips bun install and go mod tidy ; initialization preserves non-empty directories. The Zig template requires Zig 0.16.x; Rust uses stable Cargo/Rust. Build scripts are TypeScript run with Bun. bun run build builds the native library for the current machine into artifacts/lib/<target>/ . The manifest supplies its identity and release version to the Go wrapper, generated native constants, and npm package. bun run dev builds it once, then reuses it while watching Go edits. Restart after editing native code. Pure Go extensions have no native build step or artifact package. Before the packages are published, use bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts init-extension <directory> --type <type> --no-install from this checkout. Set the generated Go SDK requirement to the local go directory with a replace directive and the CLI dependency to a local file: path, then install dependencies. The generated README describes development and publishing.
Grid accepts track strings and the same Rust layout helpers on elements and style builders.
Groups actions and inputs under one roving-focus keyboard model.
Groups related fields under one legend and shared semantic state.

main.go starts native.Run and creates a window. Components and deferred construction callbacks return *ui.Element or *native.Node . Every created node is returned, assigned, or passed to a parent; implicit declaration blocks are unsupported. Split larger applications into ordinary Go packages.

Mount real SwiftUI controls inside a QuickGUI UI application. The ui.SwiftUI family embeds real macOS controls in a Go application. Ordinary QuickGUI components work without it.
Native dialogs use asynchronous callbacks. Capture the parent window while rendering and pass it explicitly to the request. A canceled open panel returns Canceled: true .

native.NewWindow(native.WindowOptions{Component: App}) creates a window with its own component owner and retained tree. Closing the window disposes its bindings, listeners, and component cleanup. Capture native.CurrentWindow() while constructing a component or handling an event when later work needs its window handle.

native.WatchFiles(paths, changed, ready) uses operating-system file notifications and returns a stop function. Register component resources with ui.OnCleanup , and retain cancellation functions for application-scoped listeners. Avoid polling when a native event or watcher is available. Extension session events stop when their session closes.

Pass an animated GIF or WebP path to ui.Image . The native decoder retains the frames and the file's repeat policy; no Go timer or per-frame signal is needed. The path must resolve to an available file, or you can pass a data URL. Package file assets with the CLI's resources option. See Image and project configuration .

Place the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ), using your CI secret store. Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. Keys use Sparkle's current base64-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 seed format and also work with Sparkle's sign_update tool. The CLI signs the finished platform artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed at its configured HTTPS URL. Feeds are per target, so architectures cannot accidentally install each other's binaries. The generated feed contains the current release; it does not generate Sparkle delta archives or staged rollouts. updates.manifest = true enables generation for every production build. macOS archives preserve framework symlinks and should contain the Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows requires makensis ; sign the installer with the configured Authenticode identity. Linux requires appimagetool to produce an updateable AppImage. Public-key mismatches, missing signing keys, missing installers, and unsupported payloads fail the build. Existing Rust users can explicitly enable the legacy updater Cargo feature for the Minisign JSON UpdateClient . It is no longer a default feature or part of the Go native core. That legacy client and its CLI manifest path remain separate from this Sparkle-compatible extension; use updater.Start , not the removed native.Updater facade.

Place this manifest beside the imported Go package's source , not just at the module root or in application configuration: Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. Choose a distinctive name; host is reserved and terminal uses its built-in typed contract. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores, without lib or a file extension. The npm package may use any valid scope or be unscoped. The manifest is limited to 16 KiB, and an application can require at most 32 extensions. The Go package declares the matching release during initialization and exposes a typed operation: RequireExtension only records a requirement. Do not load libraries, open windows, or start workers in init . Call operations after native.Run reports readiness, on the UI goroutine. Replies also run there. native.InvokeExtension sends any JSON-encodable value and returns the extension's JSON result, preserving explicit null members. Methods start with an ASCII letter and contain up to 64 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores, or hyphens. For a persistent service, call native.OpenExtension(name, options, changed, ready) and wait for its successful ready callback. Use session.Request("lookup", value, done) for a JSON result, or session.Command when only an error is needed. Each command has its own reply; events remain subscribed until session.Close() . Close on the UI goroutine when the owner is disposed. Reserve start and stop for session lifecycle. Wrap these low-level calls with typed options, events, and methods in your public package. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps , using the same entry package, target, and build tags as compilation. Transitive imports count; excluded files do not. Both the manifest and the RequireExtension call are needed: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

Plain buttons accept ui.OnClick(func() { ... }) . Use ui.OnClickEvent when you need *native.Event . Compound callbacks use typed values and include the native event when relevant. Keep UI state updates on the UI goroutine; use ui.Async for background work.

Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle 2.9.4, embedded only with the extension Windows QuickGUI NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for app exit, runs the verified installer with /S and the current install directory, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage A helper waits for app exit, replaces the user-owned AppImage atomically, and restores the old image if replacement or startup fails Linux .deb , system binaries, unpacked AppDirs, and root-owned installations report disabled ; use their package manager. A new AppImage must retain the updater import so the SDK can acknowledge startup to the helper. Linux backups are deleted only after that acknowledgement and a short startup grace period. Windows installer failures are reported; rollback remains the installer's responsibility. The portable backend supports HTTPS Sparkle RSS appcasts, raw Ed25519 enclosure signatures, semantic-version ordering, target-specific feeds, and Windows minimum-system requirements. It skips deltas and unsupported channel/rollout constraints. It does not implement every Sparkle feature. Feed reads are limited to 1 MiB, downloads to 512 MiB, and presentation notes to 16 KiB. Signatures and declared lengths are checked again by the installer helper before installation. No unsigned fallback is available.

Read matched path parameters with ui.UseParams , query values with ui.UseSearchParams , and the current location with ui.UseLocation . These return accessors; read them inside a binding when the displayed value should update. A parameter-only change keeps the matched route component mounted. A :name segment captures one path parameter. Keep reads inside text accessors: capturing params()["name"] during setup would leave the label at its initial value. Query parameters are separate from path parameters. This route initially displays quickgui and history .

Read signals directly in component text and fluent properties, such as ui.Text("Count: ", count()) and .Width(width()) . Custom components accept ordinary int , string , and struct parameters; calling LineItem(product, quantity()) preserves its live inputs. The QuickGUI CLI generates the internal getters and bindings automatically. Setup assignments such as initial := count() remain snapshots. Explicit accessors are still supported, and are required when using raw Go commands that bypass the view compiler. Event handlers batch writes automatically. Use ui.Batch for a group of writes elsewhere, and ui.CreateMemo for derived values. String and numeric signals can be children directly: ui.Text("Count: ", count) . The prefix stays retained while only the number updates. Numeric bindings use strconv ; they do not parse a format string. For a combined string property, use strconv.Itoa(count()) and concatenation inside an accessor.

Share Go components and build optional native providers for QuickGUI. An extension can be an ordinary Go package that composes QuickGUI components, or a Go package backed by a separately built native library. Start with Go when the existing UI and platform APIs cover your feature. Add a native extension when you need an optional native dependency, as the terminal and updater packages do.

Start after native.Run reports readiness, outside components. Share the handle between settings, menus, and any update banner. An updater belongs to the application, so closing a window must not close it. Call updates.Check(done) from a Check for Updates menu item, updates.Install(done) from an available-update banner, and updates.SetAutomaticChecks(enabled, done) from settings. Callbacks always run on the Go UI goroutine. State() reads the latest cached event without calling native code or polling. Initialization and commands report errors through their completion callbacks. Options can override the feed URL and public key. Windows/Linux also allow current version and identifier overrides; Sparkle reads those from the app bundle, and its public key must match the embedded SUPublicEDKey . Development builds are disabled by default, including when using a release-built native library. Use AllowDevelopment: true only with a deliberately configured test feed and disposable app bundle.

The builder stages the shared library plus Sparkle resources on macOS, or the installer helper on Windows/Linux. The CLI discovers the import transitively and fetches the exact-version extension package when necessary. End users need only the packaged application. The current npm release matrix ships macOS artifacts. Windows/Linux implementations can be built from source on their target hosts; publishing those prebuilt targets follows the framework's broader platform release support. See the runnable example and native extension contract . Sparkle configuration and appcast details are documented by Sparkle .
The CLI generates these files. Commit go.sum after resolving dependencies.

The CLI is not published yet. Start from a QuickGUI checkout and run the Go counter: To create a separate app, scaffold without installing registry packages and choose Go when prompted: In the generated quickgui.config.ts , change the defineConfig import to ../quickgui/packages/cli/src/index.ts to use the local CLI. Then run bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts dev --project ../my-app from the QuickGUI checkout. Pass --language go to init to skip the language prompt.
The concealed native editor with the same controlled contract as TextField.
The confirmation-focused dialog variant with stricter backdrop-dismissal defaults.
The generated main.go imports native for windows and ui for components. Pass the component function directly to WindowOptions.Component . Call native.Run once to start the application event loop.

The host creates its embedded surface after the owner window is mounted and closes it when removed. Declare reverse-hosted children inside the provided callback so their bindings and resources belong to that embedded window. Do not move retained nodes between windows.

The indicator is unstyled. This example keeps its outline mounted and shows the SVG only when checked. Set ReadOnly: true to preserve focus while preventing value changes from pointer or keyboard activation.
The multiline text-editing primitive, with the same controlled value contract as Input.
The NSHostingView-backed leaf that mounts one SwiftUI component tree inside QuickGUI.

The reference covers forms, pickers, layout and data, overlays, menus, and routing. examples/components contains all 42 original gallery demos, including a 5,000-row table and lazy tree. The separate examples/swift-ui gallery demonstrates native SwiftUI hosting.
The router selects components from the current application path and keeps a navigation history. Routes render native QuickGUI content in the current window.
The SwiftUI popover composes a native trigger through Render . Its content can reverse-host interactive QuickGUI components.

The watcher rebuilds your Go source and restarts the development app. The formatter gives long component calls consistent line breaks while preserving ordinary Go syntax. Production bundles are written under dist/darwin-* .

The working native-extension example pairs a Go package with a small C library named acme-echo . It builds against the standalone C ABI header , with no renderer or core crate dependency. In your own repository, use a layout such as: Vendor the small header into your project. C, C++, Rust, and other languages that export a C ABI can implement an extension. Rust extensions can vendor the equivalent extension_api.rs layouts and build a cdylib , without linking quickgui , quickgui-host , WGPU, or Taffy. The updater backend demonstrates an asynchronous service. The extension in this guide uses its own release 1.0.0 . Its descriptor, manifest, npm package, and RequireExtension version must agree. The service ABI version and table layout determine core compatibility; the extension's release does not need to match QuickGUI's release. Document the Go SDK and service ABI versions your package requires. The built-in terminal's typed rendering contract remains tied to its matching core release.

Gradient stops, width, height, padding, and other layout values do not interpolate through Transition . Unsupported transition property names are rejected. For a sliding switch thumb, use ui.Style().Transform("translateX(20px)") and ui.Style().Transition("transform 160ms ease-out") , then change the target to "translateX(0px)" when unchecked. Try the standalone example from a QuickGUI checkout: For your own consumer, add your Go module with go get , import its package, and run quickgui dev or quickgui build . Install the matching native npm package for offline or private distribution, or let the CLI fetch the exact release from the public npm registry. For development, set QUICKGUI_EXTENSION_DIR to the absolute target artifact directory. This override must contain every required library and resource, including transitive requirements. Resolution checks the explicit directory, installed npm package, then exact-version npm download; source-checkout fallback applies only to QuickGUI's built-in packages. Downloads require SHA-512 integrity, only declared artifacts are extracted, and caches include the npm package identity. Private registry downloads are not automatic; install private packages with your package manager first. Before shipping, verify these behaviors: An app without the import bundles no extension or optional backend dependencies. Adding and removing a transitive import changes a fresh bundle correctly. The bundled executable loads the extension through purego with the matching core. Missing files, names, ABI versions, release versions, and conflicting requirements produce errors. Starting, closing before startup finishes, repeated closing, cancellation, and application shutdown release every callback context and worker. Events stop after disposal. Background work never blocks the UI. Clean sessions sleep; queues, snapshots, caches, and resource payloads have limits. Follow the performance guide . bun pm pack includes every library and resource your manifest declares. Install the resulting archive into a separate consumer, build with native source staging unavailable, and exercise it on each supported OS and architecture. The repository's scripts/check-extensions.ts builds the independent C extension, exercises its real replies through purego, and bundles a separate consumer with its own Go module and npm scope. It also checks the built-in extensions and their combinations. Add equivalent checks to your extension repository. End users receive the packaged application with all selected libraries; they need no Bun, Cargo, npm packages, or native toolchain to run it.
Typography inherits through the node tree. Colors accept hex, rgb() / rgba() , or packed RGBA values. Override only the child properties that differ. Padding and borders do not inherit.

ui.Style() returns a ui.StyleBuilder . Modifiers return new values, leaving shared styles unchanged. Assign the result when deriving a style. Apply it with .Style(...) or a compound part’s PartProps.Style field; parts also accept slices of builders and accessors returning them. Scalar accessors stay reactive and bind independently on each mounted node. .When(condition, func(s ui.StyleBuilder) ui.StyleBuilder { ... }) conditionally derives a builder from a boolean value. For a reactive condition, use the element’s .When(getter, style) or evaluate the builder inside a part’s style accessor. Pass scalar signal getters to modifiers, such as .Width(width) ; calling width() during setup captures its current value.
