Use github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/native for windows and platform services, github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui for UI, and github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/reactive for owners and contexts. @quickgui/cli is a development dependency. Pin the Go SDK and CLI to compatible release versions. To share your own components or build an optional native backend, see Authoring Extensions .

Use PartProps.Style for each part. Build styles with ui.Style() and fluent modifiers; combine shared builders with .Merge(...) . Parts also accept slices of builders and accessors returning them. Selection and theme signals update retained parts without rebuilding children. Every native control has a dedicated page in the Components sidebar. For complete workflows, see Forms & Input and Overlays & Dialogs .

Use the typed native APIs for dialogs, clipboard, shell, appearance, menus, and other platform services. Operations with results use completion callbacks; handle their errors without blocking the UI goroutine. Independent extensions use native.InvokeExtension and native.OpenExtension . For application background work, use ui.Async with component cancellation or native.Dispatch to return results to the UI goroutine. Read and write signals only there. See Authoring Extensions for service and session ownership.

Use TypeScript scripts run with Bun to build native artifacts once. The example's build-extension.ts compiles its C extension directly with Clang and stages the current host target. A Rust extension can invoke Cargo from its own repository in the same way: Set the Rust library name to quickgui_acme_echo and its crate type to cdylib . Run bun build-extension.ts on each supported host. This script does not cross-compile. Target directories are darwin-arm64 , darwin-x64 , linux-arm64 , linux-x64 , windows-arm64 , and windows-x64 . Ship only targets you build and validate. The native npm package contains artifacts and exposes its metadata for the resolver: Replace @acme with your own scope. Publish this artifact package with your own release workflow and keep it optional; the Go import selects it. Your build script and releases are independent of QuickGUI's built-in --extension command and version synchronization. Consumers reuse your prebuilts during Go edits. If your extension needs helper executables or resources, declare their basenames in a manifest resources object keyed by darwin , linux , or windows . Each platform accepts up to 16 distinct files; the same platform list applies to both architectures. Put those files next to the library in every applicable target directory. The CLI copies them alongside the native libraries and marks plain resource executables as executable. Directory resources use .qgr bundles produced by the repository's packResources helper. It preserves executable modes and confined relative symlinks with entry and byte limits. Resource paths cannot overwrite core or extension images. macOS frameworks must also satisfy the platform's signing requirements. Sparkle resources receive the existing macOS signing and bundle configuration; other services do not need updater settings.

Use ui.CreateEffect to synchronize a side effect with the signals it reads. Dependencies follow the reads made during each run, including conditional branches. Register teardown with ui.OnCleanup ; disposing the owning component releases its effects and subscriptions. Bind changing text and props directly instead of rebuilding a view inside an effect. Use an effect for work outside the view tree, such as synchronizing a subscription or updating a native window title. The effect runs initially and again when a value it read changes. Cleanup registered inside that effect runs before the next execution and when its owner is disposed. This example logs the lifecycle; replace the log calls with your subscription’s start and stop operations. Capture the topic for that execution so cleanup refers to the old topic.
Use ui.CreateMemo for a value computed from other signals. It returns an accessor, so consumers subscribe to the derived value just like any other signal.

Use ui.For for a reactive list and provide stable, unique keys. Use ui.KeyedFor when retained rows need an accessor to changing item data. Removed rows release their subscriptions; moving a keyed row preserves its native identity. Virtualized tables and lists keep large collections bounded to visible rows. Use a database ID or another stable identity as the key, not an item’s position. In this example reordering moves the existing rows, and renaming item 1 updates its label through the row accessor. The parent does not recreate the list. Pass a new slice when editing data so the signal receives the update; mutating a previously stored slice in place does not notify subscribers.

Use ui.Show when state should mount or remove children. A normal Go if runs only during construction. Branch children keep their nodes while the condition stays in the same branch, and disposal removes their bindings.

Use ui.TransitionDeclaration when several properties share one timing configuration. Import time for the duration in this example. Pass longhand transition props directly to the primitive: Field Usage ui.Style().TransitionProperty(...) A comma-separated string or []string of supported property names. ui.Style().TransitionDuration(...) Milliseconds as a number, a time.Duration , or a string such as "180ms" or "0.18s" . The host bounds durations to 0–10 seconds. ui.Style().TransitionEasing(...) "linear" , "ease" , "ease-in" , "ease-out" , or "ease-in-out" . "ease" aliases the default "ease-in-out" ; these select QuickGUI curves. ui.Style().TransitionTimingFunction(...) Alias for ui.Style().TransitionEasing(...) . ui.Style().TransitionMaxFps(...) Optional frame-rate cap. Omit it to follow display presentation; completion still occurs at the transition deadline. A node has one duration, easing, and frame-rate cap for all selected properties. Comma-separated shorthand entries collect property names; the last duration and easing apply to the entire list. Delays, cubic-bezier() , and independent timings per property are not supported. Explicit longhand fields override the shorthand. A duration alone, such as ui.Style().Transition(180 * time.Millisecond) , transitions background, border, and text colors. Select "all" explicitly to include all supported paint properties. Use ui.Style().Transition("none") to remove the shorthand declaration.

Use your own Go module, npm package or scope, and release cycle. Consumers import your Go package; the CLI discovers its manifest and bundles the selected native artifact. No core registry entry, extension-specific kind, CLI fork, or QuickGUI release-pipeline change is needed. An extension runs in the application's process. The Go application loads the core and selected extensions through purego. Each extension owns its backend dependencies; the core keeps the renderer, layout engine, and native event loop. Go edits reuse these libraries, so consumers do not rebuild the native backend on every edit.

WindowOptions.Component creates one reactive root per window. Closing the window disposes its nodes and effects. Register resource cleanup with ui.OnCleanup . For background work, ui.Async delivers its result back to the UI goroutine and cancels when its component is disposed. Start background work while its component is mounting. The load function runs away from the UI goroutine and must respect its context; the completion callback can safely write signals. Removing this component’s owning branch or closing its window cancels the context and suppresses late completion. This example uses the standard context package.

Wrap related routes in ui.Layout . Its component calls ui.Outlet() where the matched child belongs. Navigation between sibling routes keeps their common layout mounted, preserving its state. Only the changed route branch is replaced. Keep shared navigation outside the outlet. Its local state survives switching between Home and Settings because both routes share the same layout. The outlet supplies only the active child.
